podcasts.title: How Fast Should We Build Superintelligence? | Nick Bostrom
podcasts.summary: The question isn’t simply whether humanity should race toward superintelligence or stop. Nick Bostrom argues the harder challenge is preserving the ability to slow down when safety falls behind, without turning a temporary pause into permanent technological stagnation. a16z’s Eddy Lazzarin and Elena Burger sit down with Bostrom to revisit the ideas he helped bring into the mainstream, now that increasingly capable AI systems actually exist. They discuss why alignment may become harder as models grow more situationally aware, which capability improvements may carry more risk than others, and why Bostrom favors “pacing the frontier” rather than committing to a broad or indefinite pause. They also examine the cost of waiting. Bostrom argues that safely developed superintelligence could radically extend human lifespans and address problems from disease to poverty, meaning delay carries risks of its own. From there, the conversation turns to Deep Utopia , governance, the possibility of post-human forms of life, the simulation argument, and whether AI could eventually surpass humans at philosophy itself. podcasts.title: Superintelligence Needs the Physical World with CEO and Co-Founder of Arda Bob McGrew
podcasts.summary: Is the AI singularity actually coming? Bob McGrew, former Chief Research Officer at OpenAI, argues that superintelligence won’t arrive without changes in the physical world, and that the “hard takeoff” argument is wrong. Sarah Guo and Elad Gil sit down with Bob, an early key executive at Palantir who later led research at OpenAI. He is now CEO and co-founder of Arda, which is leveraging AI to make American manufacturing competitive. Bob explains why automating AI researchers is a one-time boost rather than a runaway loop, and why GPUs, compute, wet labs, and factories are the real bottlenecks. They cover Arda’s work with Anduril on everything from actuators to missiles to the Fury combat aircraft, why Arda is building “Cursor for manufacturing engineers”, and how the forward deployed engineering model really works. Plus, the big-picture future view: machines that make machines, self-replicating factories, and Bob’s answer to the Fermi paradox. Sign up for new podcasts every week. podcasts.title: What Breaks When You Scale 10x? | Zipline’s Keller Cliffton
podcasts.summary: It was illegal to fly autonomously in U.S. airspace when Keller Cliffton started Zipline, so the company went somewhere that would let it prove the technology worked: Rwanda. A decade later, Zipline has made more than 3 million deliveries and is bringing its autonomous delivery network to the U.S. Keller joins Sophia Dew on The Method to explain why Zipline started by delivering blood to hospitals, how operating in the real world shaped the company, and why almost everything has to be reinvented every time the business grows 10x. They also discuss Zipline’s expansion into U.S. home delivery, how the company organizes teams more like special forces than a traditional hierarchy, and why Keller believes demand could eventually reach 50 billion instant deliveries a year in the U.S. Resources: Originally published by The Method .
